title: Review: Group 7: halogens; Reactivity series and displacement; Halide ions
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT06#t2 term and clue written for the game; RX09#t3 term and clue written for the game; RX09#t4 term and clue written for the game; PT06#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: PT05#N.16, PT06#N.3, RX09#N.2, PT05#N.11, PT06#N.5, RX09#N.6, PT05#N.3, PT06#N.10, RX09#N.8, PT05#N.7, PT06#N.14. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Nitric acid
items.clue: Added first, dilute, to remove carbonate and hydroxide without adding Cl⁻ or sulfate.

items.label: Spectator ion
items.clue: What K⁺ is when Cl₂ reacts with KBr(aq): shown in the full equation, omitted from the shorter one.

items.label: Cyclohexane
items.clue: Organic solvent shaken with the mixture; its top layer is violet with iodine, orange with bromine.

items.label: Ammonia solution
items.clue: Added last to confirm the halide: AgCl dissolves when it is dilute, AgBr only when it is concentrated.

questions.stem: Swimming pools are often disinfected by adding a white solid, Ca(ClO)₂, instead of chlorine gas. Why does it kill bacteria in the same way as chlorine does?

options.text: It releases chloride ions, which are toxic to bacteria even at low concentrations.
Its calcium ions are taken up by bacteria and stop their cells from dividing.
It gives chlorate(I) ions, the oxidising agent that chlorine forms in water.
It slowly releases chlorine gas, which kills the bacteria as it bubbles out.

questions.explanation: Ca(ClO)₂ is calcium chlorate(I). Dissolved, it gives ClO⁻ ions, which form HClO in water. These are the oxidising agents that kill bacteria, just as when Cl₂ reacts with water (Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO).

questions.stem: A student tests a solution for halide ions by adding silver nitrate solution acidified with dilute hydrochloric acid. A white precipitate forms. What can the student conclude?

options.text: The solution contains chloride ions, because AgCl is white.
The solution contains carbonate ions, because the acid did not remove them.
The solution contains no bromide or iodide, because the precipitate is not cream or yellow.
Nothing about chloride ions, because the hydrochloric acid itself added Cl⁻ ions.

questions.explanation: Right. The added Cl⁻ forms white AgCl whatever was in the sample. Repeat with dilute nitric acid.

questions.stem: Which statement about the relative ease of reduction of the halogens is correct?

options.text: Iodine is reduced more readily than bromine, as it is further down the group.
Bromine is reduced more readily than chlorine, as its nucleus has more protons.
Iodide ions are reduced more readily than iodine, as they are charged.
Chlorine is reduced more readily than bromine, as its atoms are smaller.

questions.explanation: An electron added to a chlorine atom is closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so it is held more strongly.

questions.stem: In which reaction is chlorine both oxidised and reduced?

options.text: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO
Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl

questions.explanation: One Cl atom goes from 0 to −1 (reduced) in HCl; the other goes from 0 to +1 (oxidised) in HClO. That is disproportionation.

questions.stem: An unknown sodium halide solution is acidified and silver nitrate is added. The precipitate does not dissolve in dilute ammonia solution, but does dissolve in concentrated ammonia solution. Which ion is present?

options.text: Chloride
Bromide
Iodide
Fluoride

questions.explanation: AgBr (cream) dissolves only in concentrated ammonia. That matches both results.

questions.stem: Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution: Cl₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(aq). Which statement is correct?

options.text: Iodide ions are reduced, because they lose electrons.
Chlorine is the oxidising agent, and its oxidation number falls from 0 to −1.
Chlorine is oxidised, because it forms chloride ions.
Potassium ions are oxidised, because the solution turns brown.

questions.explanation: Cl₂ gains electrons from I⁻, so it is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent.

questions.stem: At room temperature iodine is a solid but chlorine is a gas. Which statement explains this?

options.text: The I–I covalent bond is stronger than the Cl–Cl bond, so iodine molecules are harder to break up.
Iodine molecules have more electrons, so the London forces between them are stronger.
Iodine molecules are polar, so permanent dipole–dipole forces hold them together.
Iodine is more electronegative, so each molecule attracts its neighbours more strongly.

questions.explanation: I₂ has 106 electrons and Cl₂ has 34. Larger temporary dipoles form, so the intermolecular forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

questions.stem: Concentrated sulfuric acid is added separately to solid sodium bromide and to solid sodium iodide. Which product forms with sodium iodide but not with sodium bromide?

options.text: Sulfur dioxide
Hydrogen halide gas
Hydrogen sulfide
The halogen element

questions.explanation: Only iodide is a strong enough reducing agent to take sulfur from +6 all the way to −2 in H₂S (bad-egg smell).

questions.stem: A few drops of bromine water are added to a colourless solution containing both potassium chloride and potassium iodide, in excess. Cyclohexane is then added and the mixture shaken. What colour is the top layer, and why?

options.text: Pale green, because Br₂ oxidises Cl⁻ to Cl₂
Orange, because Br₂ reacts with neither halide and dissolves in the cyclohexane
Colourless, because Br₂ is reduced to colourless bromide ions
Violet, because Br₂ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ but cannot oxidise Cl⁻

questions.explanation: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂. Iodine dissolves in cyclohexane, giving violet. Cl⁻ is untouched.

questions.stem: Bromine water is added separately to aqueous potassium chloride and to aqueous potassium iodide. Which observation is expected?

options.text: A reaction occurs with the potassium chloride only
There is no reaction with either of the two solutions
A reaction occurs with both of the salt solutions
A reaction occurs with the potassium iodide only

questions.explanation: Bromine oxidises iodide ions, which are below it in Group 7: Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq), and the solution darkens to brown. Bromine cannot oxidise chloride ions.

questions.stem: A solution contains both potassium chloride and potassium iodide. Acidified silver nitrate is added until no more precipitate forms. Then excess concentrated ammonia solution is added and the mixture is shaken. What is seen at the end?

options.text: A white precipitate and a yellow precipitate both remain
A cream precipitate remains and the solution is colourless
No precipitate remains and the solution is colourless
Only a yellow precipitate remains

questions.explanation: Both AgCl and AgI form. Ammonia dissolves the AgCl but not the AgI, so the yellow precipitate is left.
